case_title: Forged Supreme Court orders digital-arrest fraud against senior citizen couple
case_number: Suo Motu Writ Petition (Criminal) No.3/2025; FIR Nos.76/2025 and 77/2025
impersonated_identity_detail: Persons impersonating CBI officers, Enforcement Directorate officials and judicial authorities; forged Supreme Court and other judicial/official orders.
initial_contact_summary: A senior-citizen couple reported being contacted between 3 and 16 September 2025 by persons impersonating CBI, Enforcement Directorate and judicial authorities through telephone and video calls.
pretext_summary: The operators displayed forged Supreme Court orders and other purported freeze, arrest, surveillance and court documents, claimed criminal investigation, and threatened arrest and property seizure under a digital-arrest pretext.
other_psychological_mechanism: High-intensity legitimacy theatre using forged judicial documents, institutional seals/signatures, and threats of criminal process/property seizure.
requested_action: Remain compliant with the purported authorities and transfer funds through multiple bank transactions under the claimed digital-arrest/investigation process.
victim_action: The couple transferred INR 10,550,000 through multiple bank transactions.
other_evidence: Forged Supreme Court freeze/arrest/surveillance materials and fictitious Bombay High Court proceedings described in the Supreme Court order; two Cyber Crime Branch Ambala FIRs.
attribution_target: Unknown CBI/ED/judicial impersonator cluster.
attribution_limitations: The procedural order establishes the complainants' reported modus operandi and the existence of FIRs but does not identify specific human operators or reproduce telecom, device, account-control or platform attribution.
primary_evidentiary_gap: Telecom/platform/device and beneficiary-account evidence identifying the human operators behind the impersonated authorities and mapping the INR 10.55 million payment path.
disposition: Supreme Court took suo motu cognizance on 17 October 2025, issued notice to central/state authorities and directed a status report from the Superintendent of Police, Cyber Crime, Ambala; the order did not adjudicate offender guilt.
case_summary: A senior-citizen couple reported a digital-arrest scam running from 3 to 16 September 2025 in which callers posed as CBI, Enforcement Directorate and judicial authorities. They displayed forged Supreme Court orders through WhatsApp/video conferencing and threatened arrest and property seizure. The couple transferred INR 10.55 million. The Supreme Court treated the forged judicial documents as sufficiently serious to initiate suo motu proceedings, but the public order does not identify the fraud operators.
research_notes: This record codes the focal complainant incident described in the Supreme Court's procedural order, not the Court's broader discussion of digital-arrest fraud as a national phenomenon.

case_title: Vodafone duplicate-SIM impersonation and INR 10.5 lakh banking fraud
case_number: Cyber Appeal Nos.6 and 7 of 2014; Cyber Complaint No.14/2013
platform_primary: Vodafone mobile service / SBI internet banking
impersonated_identity_detail: A person calling himself Kaustubh Das purported to be Prashant Buradkar's authorized representative and presented an authorization letter to request a replacement SIM.
reconnaissance_description: The impostor possessed enough subscriber identity/document information to present an authorization-based replacement request; the source does not establish how it was acquired.
initial_contact_summary: On 23 July 2011 an impostor visited a Vodafone store at Vashi, represented himself as the complainant's authorized representative and requested a replacement SIM for the complainant's registered mobile number.
pretext_summary: The impostor used a purported authorization letter and subscriber identity to obtain and activate a replacement SIM, which was then associated with unauthorized banking access and siphoning from the complainant's SBI account.
other_psychological_mechanism: Identity/authorization impersonation was directed at telecom staff to induce a service action that transferred control of the registered mobile number.
requested_action: Issue and activate a replacement SIM on the basis of the purported subscriber authorization.
victim_action: Vodafone issued and activated the replacement SIM. The complainant later alleged INR 1,050,000 was siphoned from his SBI Mahal Branch account.
other_evidence: SIM replacement form and submitted authorization/identity documents; police Section 91 request and telecom response; bank transaction material discussed in the adjudicatory record.
attribution_target: Unknown replacement-SIM impostor and downstream banking/beneficiary network.
attribution_limitations: The TDSAT judgment establishes the fraudulent replacement-SIM event and loss allegation for service-provider liability, but it does not identify the impostor as a resolved real-world human or map every downstream banking actor to that person.
alternative_explanation: A recipient/beneficiary role in the financial trail would not by itself prove the same person made the in-person SIM-replacement request.
primary_evidentiary_gap: Human identification of the impostor through store/device/CCTV or other corroboration, and transaction/login evidence linking the replacement SIM to specific online-banking sessions and beneficiaries.
disposition: TDSAT dismissed the telecom and bank appeals on 12 September 2024 and upheld/considered compensation liability arising from the 2011 replacement-SIM fraud; the proceeding did not determine criminal guilt of the unknown impostor.
case_summary: A person using the name Kaustubh Das presented himself at a Vodafone store as Prashant Buradkar's authorized representative and obtained a replacement SIM on 23 July 2011. Buradkar later alleged INR 1.05 million was siphoned from his SBI account. The TDSAT appellate judgment reconstructs the SIM-replacement documents, police information requests and banking loss while addressing telecom/bank liability. The human behind the impostor identity remains unresolved.
research_notes: The focal loss is INR 1,050,000 as stated in the adjudicatory record. Compensation figures awarded against service providers are not coded as victim loss.

case_title: Google-rating work-from-home task scam

case_summary: A WhatsApp offer for paid Google-rating work moved a victim into a Telegram and web-portal task scheme that used a small initial payout to establish trust before escalating prepaid tasks, causing INR 799,850 in loss. case_title: Hotel honeytrap and WhatsApp sextortion against cable operator
impersonated_identity_detail: A woman using the name Sukanya initiated an in-person sexual/honeytrap interaction; a later caller using the name Nandini sent the nude video and extortion demands escalated through multiple callers.
initial_contact_summary: In September 2019, cable operator Shekar met a woman calling herself Sukanya at a Bengaluru hotel, where she allegedly made him nude and recorded video.

other_psychological_mechanism: Sexual/reputational coercion using intimate imagery and threats to circulate it to social contacts.

case_summary: A Bengaluru cable operator was honeytrapped in a hotel, secretly recorded nude and later threatened by phone and WhatsApp that the video would be circulated unless he paid. He ultimately paid INR 3.4 million. The bail order links multiple accused to the scheme and alleges a conspiracy role for Arun M, but actor-specific digital attribution remains incomplete.
research_notes: Incident begins with the 2019 in-person trap and continues into 2020 extortion; exact end date is not coded.

case_title: Mumbai Police digital-arrest fraud against senior citizen

case_summary: A man in his seventies was placed under digital arrest by unknown persons posing as Mumbai Police IPS officers and induced to transfer INR 13,818,100 under a money-laundering pretext. The bail applicant was alleged to be a downstream mastermind/fund handler, but the source does not independently identify him as the victim-facing caller.

case_title: WhatsApp and Telegram part-time investment-task fraud

case_title: UBS Asset Management VIP WhatsApp investment-group fraud
platform_primary: WhatsApp / purported UBS Asset Management investment group
impersonated_identity_detail: A WhatsApp group styled 'UBS Asset Management VIP exclusive group' offering trading/investment activity.
initial_contact_summary: The complainant reported joining a WhatsApp group called 'UBS Asset Management VIP exclusive group' for trading.
pretext_summary: The group induced the complainant to invest on a trading/investment pretext, provided no repayment and demanded further payments for additional reasons.
other_psychological_mechanism: Brand/institutional legitimacy borrowing and sunk-cost escalation after substantial investment.
requested_action: Invest through the purported UBS-branded WhatsApp trading group and continue making payments.
victim_action: The complainant reported investing INR 14,800,000 and receiving no repayment. Preliminary investigation specifically traced a subset of INR 2,200,000 through layered bank accounts, including INR 4,194 reaching a V-Mart HDFC account at a remote layer.
other_evidence: NCRP complaint and preliminary bank-layer tracing: INR 2.2 million to an IDFC account, then portions through ICICI, PNB and a V-Mart HDFC account; the V-Mart account appeared in numerous NCRP complaints but was asserted to be a legitimate retail pass-through account.
attribution_target: Unknown WhatsApp investment-group operators and downstream beneficiary-account network.
attribution_limitations: The judgment is primarily an account-freeze proportionality dispute. It records the complainant's reported investment loss and a specific traced payment subset, but does not identify the WhatsApp operators or establish that remote-layer legitimate merchant accounts knowingly participated.
alternative_explanation: Receipt of INR 4,194 in V-Mart's retail collection account can reflect a legitimate customer purchase or pass-through rather than knowing participation in the investment fraud; the High Court treated blanket freezing as disproportionate.
primary_evidentiary_gap: Authenticated WhatsApp group/provider/device records identifying the operators, plus complete transaction-level tracing of the reported INR 14.8 million loss to human-controlled endpoints.
disposition: Madras High Court decided V-Mart's account-freeze challenge on 3 November 2025, restricting/proportioning the freeze while recording the underlying NCRP investment-fraud complaint and preliminary money trail; the judgment did not adjudicate the fraud operators' guilt.
case_summary: A complainant reported joining a WhatsApp group styled 'UBS Asset Management VIP exclusive group' and investing INR 14.8 million before realizing that no repayment was forthcoming and more money was being demanded. Police preliminary tracing followed a specific INR 2.2 million subset through several bank layers, with INR 4,194 reaching a V-Mart retail account. The High Court proceeding concerned proportionality of freezing that remote-layer account, so the record supports the attack and financial path more strongly than human attribution.
research_notes: Financial loss codes the complainant-reported INR 14.8 million total. INR 2.2 million is a specifically traced subset, not a replacement for the reported total. V-Mart is not coded as a fraud actor merely because a small remote-layer amount reached its account.

case_title: IGL account-upgrade phishing and credit-card fraud

case_summary: A Delhi petitioner reported a phishing call and link presented as an IGL account upgrade. After using the link, an unauthorized INR 354,690 credit-card transaction was made and a merchant EMI facility was activated without his knowledge. The public order concerns interim relief in the resulting banking dispute and does not identify the phishing operator.

case_title: Express Loan app vaccine-bait and image-blackmail fraud
impersonated_identity_detail: Express Loan / purported vaccine-loan eligibility link
initial_contact_summary: The focal complainant received SMS messages about a loan for a third Covid-19 vaccine dose, with a link for checking eligibility; clicking it downloaded the Express Loan app.

attribution_target: Express Loan operator network and account-linked downstream accused.
attribution_limitations: The bail order contains network-level CDR/IP and bank material and identifies accused linked to accounts, but not every accused is shown to have authored the focal SMS or threats to Rohan Kapoor.

primary_evidentiary_gap: Authenticated app/backend, messaging and device records mapping the focal SMS and threatening identities to specific operators.
disposition: The cited public source is a procedural bail/interim proceeding; the underlying cyber-fraud merits and offender guilt are not treated as finally adjudicated.
case_summary: A Delhi complainant clicked an SMS link framed around eligibility for a third Covid-19 vaccine dose, which installed the Express Loan app. After he entered Aadhaar and PAN details and received a small loan, operators used access to his contacts and images to threaten him with morphed photographs. The bail record documents a broader extortion network, CDR/IP tracing and beneficiary accounts.
research_notes: The separate INR 25 lakh extortion suffered by another complainant, Aditya Sharma, is not normalized as the focal victim’s loss. The wider INR 140 crore network transaction figure is also not coded as focal loss.

case_summary: A Maharashtra complainant downloaded the Handy Loan app, supplied identity and banking details and received a INR 7,147 loan. The anticipatory-bail order records CDR and co-accused material but leaves the precise victim-facing operator unresolved.
